b: Q: What is otitis externa?
Inflammation/infection of the external auditory canal
Also called "swimmer's ear"
Bacterial: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus (most common)
Fungal: Aspergillus, Candida

snip.t: Malignant otitis externa — especially in diabetics and immunosuppressed

faq.a: It thrives in moist environments; water exposure creates a perfect niche in the canal.
faq.q: Why is Pseudomonas the most common bacteria?

faq.a: Only if complications like necrotising disease damage the canal or middle ear; prompt treatment usually prevents this.
faq.q: Can otitis externa cause permanent hearing loss?

faq.a: Yes, for necrotising otitis externa, diabetic or immunocompromised patients, or when topical therapy fails.

exam: What bedside signs differentiate otitis externa from otitis media? — Look for canal edema, pain on tragus traction, and a normal tympanic membrane.
A diabetic patient presents with severe ear pain and granulation tissue in the canal. What is your next step? — Start systemic anti‑pseudomonal therapy and arrange urgent ENT imaging.
Why are topical steroid‑antibiotic drops preferred over oral antibiotics for uncomplicated disease? — They deliver high local concentration, avoid systemic side effects, and reduce inflammation.
How would you manage otitis externa in a setting without culture facilities? — Empiric topical ciprofloxacin‑dexamethasone, clean the canal, and monitor response.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt immediate referral? — New facial nerve palsy or spreading cellulitis beyond the ear.
Explain why cotton‑bud cleaning can precipitate otitis externa. — It disrupts the protective cerumen barrier and creates micro‑abrasions for bacterial entry.
When is systemic antifungal therapy indicated? — In refractory fungal otitis externa after failure of topical agents or in immunocompromised patients.
What preventive advice reduces recurrence in swimmers? — Keep ears dry, use ear plugs, and avoid inserting objects into the canal.
ai.title: Otitis Externa
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Inflammation of the external auditory canal, usually bacterial, presenting with ear pain and discharge. Recognise severity, common tropical causes, and manage promptly to avoid complications.

b: Pain worsens with tragus traction or pinna movement
Canal appears swollen, red, and may have debris
sections.p: Otitis externa is inflammation of the external auditory canal, often infectious. Diagnosis is clinical: painful ear, canal erythema, edema, and purulent or serous discharge.

b: Mild: erythema, mild edema, no discharge
Moderate: edema, discharge, pain with movement
Severe (necrotising): extensive edema, ulceration, granulation tissue, possible skull base involvement
sections.p: Severity is graded by canal edema and presence of complications:

b: Bacterial: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (most common), Staphylococcus aureus
Fungal: Aspergillus spp., Candida spp. (especially after prolonged antibiotic use)
Trauma: cotton‑bud injury, ear cleaning, water exposure
Underlying disease: diabetes, HIV, chronic ear eczema
sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings the most frequent aetiologies are:

b: Pain aggravated by pulling on the pinna
Mild fever only in severe or necrotising forms
Hearing loss is usually conductive and transient
sections.p: Typical presentation includes acute ear pain, itching, and discharge. Systemic signs are absent unless complications develop.
Investigations are guided by severity and resource availability.

t.b: Confirms canal inflammation and identifies discharge; essential for diagnosis
Answers which pathogen is present; guides antibiotic choice when available
Detects bone erosion or skull‑base involvement; if unavailable, refer for specialist assessment
Detects diabetes, a risk factor for necrotising disease

b: Severe, unrelenting pain despite analgesia
Granulation tissue or ulceration in the canal
Cranial nerve palsies (facial nerve)
Systemic signs: high fever, sepsis
sections.p: Complications are rare but life‑threatening; watch for:

b: Topical antibiotic‑steroid drops (e.g., ciprofloxacin‑dexamethasone) – first line for bacterial disease
If fungal suspected, topical antifungal (clotrimazole) after cleaning canal
Analgesia: oral NSAIDs or paracetamol
Diabetics or immunocompromised with necrotising disease: systemic anti‑pseudomonal antibiotics (e.g., ciprofloxacin) plus ENT referral
Avoid systemic steroids unless indicated for another condition
sections.p: Treat the cause, relieve pain, and prevent spread.

b: Educate on keeping ear dry (use ear plugs after bathing)
Avoid cotton‑bud cleaning
Control diabetes and HIV viral load
Treat underlying eczema or dermatitis
sections.p: Re‑examine after 3‑5 days; ensure symptom resolution.

b: Otitis media – pain deeper, tympanic membrane bulges
Eczema of the external canal – chronic itching, no purulent discharge
Cerumen impaction – blockage, but no canal edema
Negative swab does not rule out infection if sample is inadequate
Normal temperature does not exclude necrotising disease in diabetics
Ear pain may be referred from temporomandibular joint disorders

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid spread of swelling, facial nerve weakness
High fever or signs of sepsis
